nameStory: The common loon gets its name from its haunting, wailing calls that echo across northern lakes - sounds that early settlers thought resembled the cries of a lunatic or 'loon.' The word 'loon' likely comes from the Scandinavian word 'lom,' meaning a lame or clumsy person, referring to how awkwardly these water-adapted birds move on land.
description: The common loon is a large, striking waterbird that's perfectly built for life on New England's lakes and coastal waters. About the size of a small goose, these elegant divers are famous for their haunting calls and dramatic black-and-white breeding plumage. In summer, breeding adults sport a distinctive checkerboard pattern on their backs, a jet-black head with an iridescent green sheen, and a bold white 'necklace' around their throat. They're powerful underwater hunters with dagger-like bills and legs positioned far back on their bodies for maximum swimming efficiency.

idTips.label: Distinctive calls
idTips.description: Four distinct vocalizations including the famous haunting wail that carries for miles across water, plus tremolo 'laughter,' yodel, and hoot calls

idTips.label: Breeding plumage pattern
idTips.description: Bold black-and-white checkerboard or spotted pattern on the back, jet-black head with greenish iridescent sheen, and bright white underparts with a white 'necklace'

idTips.label: Body shape and posture
idTips.description: Sits low in the water with just head and back visible, torpedo-shaped body, and holds head level rather than angled up like many waterfowl

idTips.label: Diving behavior
idTips.description: Disappears completely underwater with a smooth forward dive (no splash), can stay submerged for up to a minute while hunting fish

idTips.label: Winter appearance
idTips.description: Brownish-grey above and white below with unclear shoulder patterns, dark neck and head, much plainer than breeding plumage but still distinctly loon-shaped

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with steady, powerful wingbeats and neck extended straight out, often calling while flying; requires long takeoff run across water surface

habitat: Common loons breed on clear, deep freshwater lakes throughout northern New England, preferring undeveloped waters with rocky or marshy shorelines for nesting. During winter months, they move to coastal waters along New England's Atlantic shore, including protected bays, harbors, and nearshore ocean areas. They need large bodies of water for their lengthy takeoff runs and prefer areas with good fish populations and minimal human disturbance.

seasonality.spring: Loons return to breeding lakes in April-May, immediately establishing territories and beginning their spectacular courtship displays with synchronized swimming and calling. Listen for their territorial yodel calls echoing across still morning waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak time to observe loons in full breeding plumage on northern lakes, often seen with fuzzy gray chicks riding on their backs. Adults are most vocal during early summer territorial establishment and can be observed diving frequently for fish.
seasonality.fall: Breeding plumage begins molting to duller winter colors, and loons become less vocal as they prepare for migration to coastal waters. Young birds take their first flights to wintering grounds before lakes freeze.
seasonality.winter: Look for loons in their plain brownish winter plumage along New England's coast, often in small groups in protected bays and harbors. They're generally quiet during this season but still dive actively for fish.

funFact: Loon chicks can dive underwater when they're just a few days old, but they often hitch rides on their parents' backs - not just for warmth and protection, but because mom or dad can actually dive underwater with the chick still clinging on, creating a living submarine!
confusionNotes: In winter plumage, loons might be confused with large grebes, but loons have thicker necks, larger heads, and sit much lower in the water. Remember: loons are 'low riders' - they float with barely their back showing, while grebes sit higher up like floating corks.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name 'common' loon, these birds are actually indicators of healthy, undisturbed lake ecosystems and have declined in many areas due to development pressure. In New England, they're considered a symbol of wilderness and are protected by various conservation efforts to maintain quiet zones around nesting areas.
compareHints: Common loons are much larger than red-throated loons, their only regular loon relative in New England waters. Red-throated loons have a thinner bill, gray (not black) head in breeding plumage, and can take off from water without the long runway that common loons require. Common loons also have more dramatic black-and-white patterning and much more powerful, haunting calls compared to the quieter red-throated species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red-throated loons are much smaller and more delicate-looking than Common Loons, with a thinner neck and that characteristic upward-tilted bill.
Pacific Loons are the 'Goldilocks' of their family - not as large and blocky as Common Loons, not as small and delicate as Red-throated Loons, but just right in between.
Yellow-billed Loons dwarf their Common Loon cousins in size and have that unmistakable straight yellow bill versus the Common Loon's dark, slightly curved bill.
